title: We Attribute Personalities to Chatbots, Even When We Know Better - Nautilus
gist: Users attribute distinct personalities to chatbots even knowing they are software — Claude as an overly thoughtful people-pleaser, Grok as contrarian and sometimes offensive — an instance of the ELIZA effect first observed by Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s.

insights.claim: Users rapidly perceive chatbots as having a specific temperament, even after only a few minutes of conversation and despite knowing better.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Perceived personality drives user attachment and retention, making persona design a competitive moat for AI products.
insights.quote: you may begin to feel that someone is in there, a person-shaped thing with a specific temperament
insights.locator: Talk to a chatbot for even

insights.claim: Anthropic's Claude is characterized as an overly thoughtful, library-bound colleague who above all aims to please.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Brand personality perception shapes enterprise vs. consumer positioning among AI labs.
insights.quote: an overly thoughtful colleague, who spends too much time in the library and above all, aims to please

insights.claim: xAI's Grok is characterized as direct, contrarian, anti-woke and occasionally egregiously offensive.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Edgy persona differentiates Grok but carries brand-safety and regulatory risk.
insights.quote: direct, contrarian, anti-woke and on occasion egregiously offensive

insights.claim: The tendency to anthropomorphize chatbots is called the ELIZA effect, named after the first chatbot created by MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: The effect is decades-old and robust, suggesting anthropomorphization of AI is a durable demand driver, not a fad.

insights.claim: Weizenbaum observed that most ELIZA users quickly anthropomorphized the program and shared deeply personal secrets with it.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Users' willingness to disclose to bots raises privacy and data-handling stakes for AI companions.
insights.quote: most users quickly anthropomorphized the program, sharing deeply personal secrets with it
